# Esukārī Sutta (MN 96 (PTS MN ii 177))

**ID:** MN 96 (PTS MN ii 177)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Esukārī Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Esukārī
**PTS:** MN ii 177
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Esukārī Sutta* (MN 96) is the ninety-sixth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The dialogue occurs between the Buddha and the brahmin householder Esukāri, who approaches the Buddha to defend the brahminical view of social hierarchy and privilege [Dutt; McTighe; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Esukāri propounds that birth determines social division, positing four grades of service—whereby a brahmin can be served by all four classes, a kshatriya by three, a vaiśya by two, and a śūdra solely by another śūdra—alongside four corresponding types of hereditary wealth [Thomas 1933; Hazra 1994; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha counters that one's true worth depends on conduct rather than caste [Hazra 1994]. He teaches that service should be evaluated purely on ethical and spiritual outcomes: one ought to serve someone only if such service increases faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom [Thomas 1933; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Furthermore, he identifies the noble Dhamma as a person's true wealth [McTighe]. Using the simile of kindling fire, the Buddha explains that just as fire ignited from different types of wood possesses the same heat, flame, and brightness, members of any caste who go forth are equally capable of accomplishing the wholesome Dhamma [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Priestley 1999]. Convinced, Esukāri declares himself a lay follower [Dutt; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

Anesaki notes that the Chinese counterpart is longer and includes a shepherd simile absent from the Pali recension [Anesaki 1908].

- [Dutt] Nalinaksha Dutt, Early History of the Spread of Buddhism and the Buddhist Schools — Context on Esukāri as a Sāvatthi brahmin who converted to the Buddha's teachings.
- [McTighe] McTighe, Mentoring in the Majjhima Nikaya — Categorization of Esukāri as a brahmin householder, claims of caste service, and teaching on Dhamma as true wealth.
- [Thomas 1933] Edward J. Thomas, The History of Buddhist Thought (1933) — Analysis of Esukāri's claims regarding caste-based service and the Buddha's refutation.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Summary of Esukāri's criterion of birth and the Buddha's rejection of it.
- [Priestley 1999] Leonard C.D.C. Priestley, Pudgalavāda Buddhism (1999) — Discussion of the fire simile in the Esukārī Sutta regarding social status and fuels.
- [Anesaki 1908] Masaharu Anesaki, The Four Buddhist Āgamas in Chinese (1908) — Comparison with the Chinese Āgama counterpart and identification of the unique shepherd simile.
